### B.1 Motivation

In general, estimating posterior-based quantities tends to follow two approaches:

- 1. Sampling-based (i.e. Monte Carlo) approaches.

- 2. Grid-based (i.e. “brute force”) approaches.

Both have benefits and drawbacks, which we discuss briefly below.

Monte Carlo methods such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo [12, 100, 52, 106, MCMC;] or Nested Sampling [101, 102] try to characterize the posterior distribution $P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ by generating a set of $n$ samples $\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ along with a set of corresponding weights $\{w_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ . Expectation values (i.e. weighted averages) of functions $f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ taken over the posterior

$$ \mathbb{E}_{{P}}\left[{f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}\right]\equiv\int f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi}){\rm d}\boldsymbol{\theta}\,{\rm d}\boldsymbol{\phi} $$

can then be estimated via:

$$ \mathbb{E}_{{P}}\left[{f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}\right]\approx\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\times f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}} $$

While Monte Carlo methods allow us to in theory derive arbitarily precise estimates for $\mathbb{E}_{{P}}\left[{f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}\right]$ , they suffer from two main drawbacks when trying to infer stellar properties from photometry:

- 1. Many of the posterior distributions for stars have multiple, widely-separated solutions due to the “dwarf-giant degeneracy” since main sequence (MS) stars (“dwarfs”) and post-MS stars (“giants”) can often have similar colors but very different luminosities. Many Monte Carlo methods struggle to characterize these types of multi-modal distributions efficiently.

- 2. We expect most posteriors to have extended and complex degeneracies since changes in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ (e.g., $T_{\rm eff}$ and $A_{V}$ ) can impact observables in similar ways. Accurately characterizing these uncertainties will require more samples and/or longer run-times from Monte Carlo methods.

“Brute force” methods can get around these problem by computing the posterior probability $P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ over a large grid of $n$ values $\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ . These can then be used to estimate the expectation value in a similar way to our initial set of samples via

$$ \mathbb{E}_{{P}}\left[{f(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}\right]\approx\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta_{i}\times P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})\times f(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Delta_{i}\times P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})} $$

where $\Delta_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Delta_{i,j}$ is the volume of each element $i$ of the grid with spacing $\Delta_{i,j}$ for the $j$ -th parameter (out of $m$ total) at position $(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i})$ . For an evenly-spaced grid in each parameter, $\Delta_{i}=\Delta$ is constant.

While grids scale extremely poorly ( $\propto e^{p}$ ) as the number of parameters $p$ increases, for $p\lesssim 4$ parameters grids often only comprise $\sim 10^{6}$ elements that can be fit extremely quickly using modern computing architectures that excel at linear algebra operations. This often makes evaluating grids 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than sequentially generating samples via Monte Carlo methods. It also allows grids to be expansive enough to explore large regions of parameter space at fine enough resolution to characterize multiple modes robustly.

Unfortunately, when inferring stellar properties from photometry the number of parameters $p$ is often $\gtrsim 5$ . To get around this, grid-based approaches often either simplify the problem (see §II.1.1) and/or apply grids to only a few parameters at a time. This, however, often can underestimate uncertainties and possibly miss solutions.

To resolve these various difficulties, brutus adopts a hybrid approach that exploits properties of our statistical model to combine grids, linear regression, and Monte Carlo methods to approximate the posterior. This allows us to exploit grids when possible to explore widely-separated modes while retaining the ability to construct accurate estimates of particular inferred quantities. These are described in more detail in the subsequent sections.

### B.2 Linear Regression in Magnitudes

The core of our approach centers on the fact that our initial model is essentially linear in the extrinsic parameters $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ since

$$ \mu+A_{V}\times(\mathbf{R}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+R_{V}\times\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\equiv\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} $$

where we have slightly abused notation by defining the $3\times 1$ vector

$$ \boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}=\begin{bmatrix}\mu\\
A_{V}\\
A_{V}\times R_{V}\end{bmatrix} $$

and

$$ \mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{1}\\
\mathbf{R}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\\
\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\end{bmatrix} $$

is the $3\times b$ “data-generating” matrix where $\mathbf{1}=\{1\}_{i=1}^{i=b}$ .

Assuming our errors $\boldsymbol{\sigma}_{\mathbf{m}}$ on the magnitudes $\hat{\mathbf{m}}$ are approximately Normal and defining $\Delta\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\equiv\hat{\mathbf{m}}-\mathbf{M}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ , the corresponding log-likelihood at fixed $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is then

$$ \displaystyle-2\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}|\boldsymbol{\theta})=\left[\Delta\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right]^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{m}}^{-1}\left[\Delta\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right]+\ln\left[{\rm det}\left(2\pi\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{m}}\right)\right] $$

If we want to solve for the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) for $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}$ , we set the $3\times 1$ Jacobian vector $\partial\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}/\partial\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}=\mathbf{0}$ and solve this linear system for $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}$ . This gives

$$ \boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\left(\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{m}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\mathrm{T}}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{m}}^{-1}\Delta\hat{\mathbf{m}}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} $$

Note that this is the standard solution for a weighted least-squares linear regression problem.

This result immediately implies that the conditional likelihood of $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ given $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}|\boldsymbol{\theta})=\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\times{\rm det}\left[2\pi\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right]}_{\rm Normalization}\times\underbrace{\mathcal{N}\left[{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})},{\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\right]}_{\rm Distribution} $$

In other words, $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}$ is Normally distributed about the MLE $\phi_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with a maximum amplitude of

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\equiv\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})) $$

and a covariance of

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \displaystyle=\left(\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{m}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\mathrm{T}}\right)^{-1} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial^{2}\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}|\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{2}}\right)^{-1} $$

where $\partial^{2}\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm mag}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}|\boldsymbol{\theta})/\partial\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{2}$ is the $3\times 3$ Hessian matrix whose elements are comprised of all the second-order derivatives. This correspondence between the covariance and the Hessian is a generic feature for Normal likelihoods. An example of this covariance structure in $(\mu,A_{V},R_{V})$ is shown on the left side of Figure 18.

Given a prior/independent constraint $\pi(\boldsymbol{\phi})=\mathcal{N}\left[{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})},{\mathbf{C}_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\right]$ on our extrinsic parameters that are Normally distributed around mean $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with covariance $\mathbf{C}_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ , the corresponding posterior can also be shown to be Normal with a mean equal to the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate by solving

$$ \displaystyle\left[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right]^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})+[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]^{-1}\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

where the (inverse) covariance is now

$$ \left[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\right]^{-1}=[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]^{-1}+[\mathbf{C}_{\rm mag}^{\pi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})]^{-1} $$

Unfortunately, we do not have (Normal) priors/independent constraints on $\mu$ , $A_{V}$ , and $A_{V}\times R_{V}$ , but rather on $\varpi$ , $A_{V}(d|\ell,b)$ , and $R_{V}$ separately. This poses a problem, since in practice we find that the MLE solution is unstable without independent constraints on $R_{V}$ , with the reddening vector able to adjust to nonphysical values to better model the data.

We resolve this by breaking our problem into two parts. First, we neglect the contribution of any constraints on $\mu$ or $A_{V}$ , which are not Normal here, and only consider our prior $\pi(R_{V})$ . Then, we exploit the fact that this system of equations is linear in $(\mu,A_{V})$ at fixed $R_{V}$ . Likewise, it is linear in $(\mu,R_{V})$ at fixed $A_{V}$ . To find $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MLE}$ , we therefore alternate between

- • solving for $(\mu,A_{V})_{\rm MLE}$ at fixed $R_{V}$ , including the contribution from $\pi(R_{V})$ , and

- • solving for $(\mu,R_{V})_{\rm MLE}$ at fixed $A_{V}$ .1414 14 brutus can also incorporate Normal priors on $A_{V}$ if desired.

We iterate between the two until both $A_{V}$ and $R_{V}$ converge to within $\delta_{A_{V}}=\delta_{R_{V}}=0.05$ , which typically occurs within a handful of iterations. Our strategy for incorporating parallax measurements and other priors is described in §B.4 and §B.6.

### B.3 Linear Regression in Flux Density

Above, we have assumed that the photometric errors are Normally distributed in magnitudes (i.e. log-flux). This is a reasonable approximation when the errors are small ( $\lesssim 5\%$ ), but lead to estimates and errors for parameters that are slightly different than when we assume errors are distributed following a Normal distribution in flux density.

For small changes $\Delta A_{V}$ and $\Delta R_{V}$ around a given value of $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ , we can Taylor expand our previous linear model in magnitudes to get a model that is linear in flux density

$$ \mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi})\approx s\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\odot\,\left[1-\frac{\ln 10}{2.5}\Delta A_{V}\left(\mathbf{R}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}+\Delta R_{V}\mathbf{R}^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\right)\right] $$

where $\odot$ here indicates the Hadamard product (i.e. element-wise multiplication), $\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is the “absolute” model flux density derived from the absolute model magnitudes $\mathbf{M}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ , and $s$ is now a scale factor that adjusts the normalization. Slightly abusing notation again and defining our parameters of interest to be

$$ \Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}\equiv\begin{bmatrix}s\\
-s\frac{\ln 10}{2.5}\Delta A_{V}\\
-s\frac{\ln 10}{2.5}\Delta A_{V}\Delta R_{V}\end{bmatrix} $$

we can again rewrite the above model in matrix form as

$$ \mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux})\approx(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux})^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}} $$

where

$$ \mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\\
\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\\
\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\\
\end{bmatrix}\,\odot\,\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{1}\\
\mathbf{R}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\\
\mathbf{R}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}^{\prime}\\
\end{bmatrix} $$

Our log-likelihood then is

$$ \displaystyle-2\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm flux}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}|\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})=\left[\hat{\mathbf{F}}-(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux})^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right]^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1}\left[\hat{\mathbf{F}}-(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux})^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\right]+\ln\left[{\rm det}\left(2\pi\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{F}}\right)\right] $$

As §B.2, this implies the conditional likelihood is analytic such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm flux}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}|\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})=\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})\times{\rm det}\left[2\pi\mathbf{C}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})\right]}_{\rm Normalization}\times\underbrace{\mathcal{N}\left[{\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})},{\mathbf{C}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}\right]}_{\rm Distribution} $$

where $\mathcal{L}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ is again evaluated at the MLE, the mean is

$$ \Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})=\left(\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\mathrm{T}}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1}\hat{\mathbf{F}} $$

and the covariance is

$$ \mathbf{C}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MLE}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})=\left(\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}\mathbf{C}_{\mathbf{F}}^{-1}\mathbf{D}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\mathrm{T}}\right)^{-1} $$

As with §B.2, in the presence of (Normal) priors/independent constraints, the MAP estimates $\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ and $\mathbf{C}_{\rm flux}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ are straightforward to derive. Similarly, due to the constraints on $R_{V}$ needed for the solution to be well-behaved, we solve for elements of $\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}$ iteratively conditioning on $A_{V}$ and $R_{V}$ in turn.

As the data $\hat{\mathbf{F}}$ are fundamentally in flux density space, we are ultimately interested in constraining our parameters relative to our linear model in flux density $\mathbf{F}_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi})$ . We therefore will redefine our earlier set of extrinsic parameters as

$$ \boldsymbol{\phi}\equiv\begin{bmatrix}s\\
A_{V}\\
R_{V}\end{bmatrix} $$

where the only change relative to our original parameters is that now we are inferring the scale-factor $s$ rather than the distance modulus $\mu$ . Note that it is straightforward to convert from $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}$ and $\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}$ to $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm flux}$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ . Around the true MAP solution $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ where $\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}=(0,0,0)$ , we can compute $\mathbf{C}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ by explicitly computing the corresponding Hessian matrix of second-order derivatives. An example showing the covariance structure in $(s,A_{V},R_{V})$ versus that in $(\mu,A_{V},R_{V})$ from §B.2 is shown in Figure 18.

Altogether, this gives us a straightforward recipe for “optimizing” our initial MAP solution, derived from magnitudes, to the corresponding distribution in flux:

- 1. Starting from an initial guess of $A_{V}=1$ , $R_{V}=3.32$ , derive $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ . Iterate in $(\mu,A_{V})$ and $(\mu,R_{V})$ until convergence.

- 2. Convert from $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm mag}^{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\rightarrow\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ and expand around $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ to derive $F_{\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi})$ .

- 3. Compute first order corrections $\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ for $s$ , $A_{V}$ , and $R_{V}$ .

- 4. Compute the new MAP solution $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}^{\rm new}=\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}+\Delta\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ .

- 5. Repeat steps 2-4 starting from $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}^{\rm new}$ until the likelihood converges.

In general, we find the likelihood quickly converges after only a handful of iterations.

### B.4 Incorporating Priors with Importance Sampling

We are interested in estimating expectation values (see §B.1) over the conditional posterior

$$ P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})=\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta})\mathcal{L}_{\rm astr}(\boldsymbol{\phi})\pi(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}) $$

From our above calculations, we now have an analytic approximation for $\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ . Critically, we now know that, conditional on $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ , $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ is approximately distributed as

$$ \boldsymbol{\phi}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\sim\mathcal{N}\left[{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})},{\mathbf{C}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\right] $$

and therefore easy to simulate. Given a set of $m$ independently and identically distributed (iid) samples $\{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=m}\sim\mathcal{N}\left[{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})},{\mathbf{C}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})}\right]$ drawn from this Normal distribution at a particular value $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$ , we can then approximate expectation values over posterior using a Monte Carlo approach through Importance Sampling via

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{P}}\left[{f(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})}\right] \displaystyle=\int f(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})\,{\rm d}\boldsymbol{\phi} \displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}q_{i,j}\times f(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{j}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}) $$

where the importance weight $q_{i,j}$ for each sample $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,j}$ is defined as

$$ q_{i,j}\equiv\frac{P(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{j}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})}{\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{j}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})}=\mathcal{L}_{\rm astr}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{j})\pi(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{j}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}) $$

Generally, we find that for $n_{\rm prior}\gtrsim 30$ samples our estimates of the integrated conditional probability for a particular model

$$ q_{i}\equiv\int P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})\,{\rm d}\boldsymbol{\phi}\approx\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}q_{i,j} $$

tend to roughly converge. As a result, we choose $n_{\rm prior}=50$ as the default number of samples in our computations. This step, which requires generating a large number of samples for every un-clipped model in our initial grid and subsequently evaluating the astrometric likelihood and Galactic prior for each sample, typically takes up the majority of the computation time.

### B.5 Application over Stellar Parameter Grids

Above, we showed that we can analytically solve for the conditional likelihood $\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta})$ , which implies that we should be able to generate estimates for those parameters without the use of grids over $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ . This allows us to both substantially improve our resolution in both $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (over our grid) and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ (with analytic sampling). In addition, we simultaneously decrease the required computation since we only require a grid of $n$ values $\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ over the $m\lesssim 4$ intrinsic set of stellar parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ rather than over the $m+3$ parameters from both $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ and $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ .

We can exploit such a grid by noting that our original posterior can be rewritten as

$$ P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})=P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi}) $$

for a given $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ . This then implies that we can generate random samples from our joint likelihood in two steps. First, we draw a random sample $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}$ from $P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ . Then, we draw a corresponding random sample $\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\prime}$ from $P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ . More formally,

$$ \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime} \displaystyle\sim P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi}) \displaystyle\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\prime} \displaystyle\sim P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi}) $$

We exploit the weighted Monte Carlo samples from §B.4 to perform this operation using a bootstrap approximation. For a particular grid point $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$ , generating a random sample $\boldsymbol{\phi}^{\prime}$ from the conditional posterior $P(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ is roughly equivalent to picking one of the already-generated set of $m$ samples $\{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}$ with a probability proportional to its weight $q_{i,j}$ . More formally, this implies

$$ \boldsymbol{\phi}^{\prime}\sim{\rm Cat}\left[\{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{j=m},\{q_{i,j}/q_{i}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}\right] $$

where ${\rm Cat}[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{p}]$ is the Categorical distribution over $\mathbf{x}=\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}=\{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,j}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}$ with corresponding probabilities $\mathbf{p}=\{p_{j}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}=\{q_{i,j}/q_{i}\}_{j=1}^{j=m}$ and again $q_{i}=\sum_{j}q_{i,j}$ is the total conditional probability.

Likewise, we can approximate drawing a sample $\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}$ from $P(\boldsymbol{\theta}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ using the same strategy by taking

$$ \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\prime}\sim{\rm Cat}\left[\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n},\{p_{i}/p\}_{i=1}^{i=n}\right] $$

The prior-weighted probability $p_{i}$ corresponding to a given $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$ is related to our previous $q_{i}$ via

$$ p_{i}\equiv q_{i}\times\pi_{i}\times\Delta_{i} $$

where $\pi_{i}=\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ is the prior probability evaluated at $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$ and $\Delta_{i}$ is the associated grid spacing. The normalization

$$ p\equiv\sum_{i}p_{i}\approx\int P(\boldsymbol{\phi},\boldsymbol{\theta}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi}){\rm d}\boldsymbol{\phi}{\rm d}\boldsymbol{\theta} $$

is then the estimated marginal likelihood (i.e. the Bayesian evidence) for the source, which in theory may be useful for model comparisons in future applications.

Using this strategy, we post-process our MAP fits and Monte Carlo samples over our grid points to generate $n_{\rm post}=250$ $\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{k})\}_{k=1}^{k=n_{\rm post}}$ samples that serve as rough approximations to the underlying posterior $P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}},\hat{\varpi})$ . In particular, we wish to emphasize that these options only generate approximations to the underlying posterior. We expect the largest differences between the estimated posterior relative to the true distribution will be primarily due to

- • grid resolution effects in $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ ,

- • “posterior noise” caused by noisy estimates of the $p_{i}$ ’s, and

- • “resampling noise” due to the procedure used to resample the final set of $n_{\rm post}$ samples.

See §VI for examples of the impact these may have on inferring underlying relevant intrinsic and extrinsic stellar properties. An example of the output stellar parameters and the associated SED can be seen in Figure 7.

#### B.6.1 Magnitude Step

While models that are reasonable fits to the data generally converge quickly, the $A_{V}$ and $R_{V}$ values for models that are poor fits can sometimes be ill-behaved. As a result, we only worry about convergence for objects with likelihoods whose values are greater than $f_{\rm tol}^{\rm mag}=0.005$ times the maximum value after the first linear regression step. We consider our fits converged when the maximum variation in $A_{V}$ and $R_{V}$ over these “reasonably fit” models falls below $\delta_{A_{V}}=0.05\,{\rm mag}$ and $\delta_{R_{V}}=0.05$ , respectively, between one iteration and the next. This usually occurs within $\lesssim 5$ iterations.

#### B.6.2 Flux Density Step

After our magnitude fits have converged, we only want to perform additional optimization after expanding in flux density for a smaller subset of grid points, indexed by $i$ , that give “good” likelihoods. Using the MLE values for $\{\boldsymbol{\phi}_{{\rm MLE},i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ , we compute the corresponding photometric likelihood $\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{{\rm MLE},i})$ and, if it is measured, an astrometric likelihood $\mathcal{L}_{\rm astr}(\boldsymbol{\phi}_{{\rm MLE},i})$ for each object. We only perform the subsequent flux density expansion and optimization for objects with combined astro-photometric likelihoods that are within $f_{\rm init}^{\rm flux}=0.005$ times the maximum value. This further screens models that may provide good fits to the photometry but give inconsistent parallax estimates.

As with our magnitude step, we only consider convergence over a set of “reasonably fit” models with likelihoods greater than $f_{\rm tol}^{\rm flux}=0.01$ the current maximum value in order to avoid being overly-sensitive to the worst-fit models under consideration (i.e. to decrease our sensitivity to the likely tails of the distribution). We take our fits to be converged after the change in the photometric log-likelihood $\ln\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{{\rm MLE},i})$ between iterations falls below $\delta_{\mathcal{L}}=0.03$ . As in §B.6.1, this usually occurs within $\lesssim 5$ iterations.

#### B.6.3 Monte Carlo Step

Since generating samples for all of our models is both time-consuming and memory-intensive over large grids, we only want to perform this step (and the subsequent resampling) over a small subset of models. We subselect these based on their “expected” posterior probabilities, which we compute in two steps.

First, we ignore all distance-dependent effects such as our 3-D priors over stellar properties and dust extinction. The remaining “static” contributions of our prior are then direct functions of our underlying grid of stellar parameters $\{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ and can therefore be pre-computed. This includes contributions from the spacing of our grid points $\{\Delta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ (see §B.1) and the associated IMF prior over mass $\pi(M_{\rm init})$ .

Second, we again want to incorporate possible constraints from the measured parallax. Unlike in §B.6.2, however, we now want to incorporate uncertainties $\sigma_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ in the inferred scale-factor $s(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ for a particular model $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}$ . The marginal distribution of $s(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ derived from $\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\phi}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ is Normal:

$$ s(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})\sim\mathcal{N}\left[{\mu_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})},{\sigma_{s}^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})}\right] $$

where $\mu_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ and $\sigma_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ are just taken from the appropriate elements of $\boldsymbol{\phi}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ and $\mathbf{C}_{\rm MAP}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ . It is straightforward to show that the inferred scale-factor $s(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ is simply the square of the associated parallax $\varpi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ :

$$ s(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})=\varpi^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i}) $$

In the case where the measured parallax $\hat{\varpi}$ is Normally distributed with at least a moderate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (i.e. $\hat{\varpi}/\sigma_{\varpi}\gg 1$ ), it is straightforward to show that the $\varpi^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})$ is also expected to be approximately Normally distributed such that

$$ \varpi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})\sim\mathcal{N}\left[{\hat{\varpi}},{\sigma_{\varpi}^{2}}\right]\quad\Rightarrow\quad\varpi^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i})\sim\mathcal{N}\left[{\mu_{\varpi^{2}}},{\sigma_{\varpi^{2}}^{2}}\right] $$

where $\mu_{\varpi^{2}}=\hat{\varpi}^{2}+\sigma_{\varpi}^{2}$ and $\sigma_{\varpi^{2}}=2\sigma_{\varpi}^{4}+4\hat{\varpi}^{2}\sigma_{\varpi}^{2}$ . We take our likelihood $\mathcal{L}_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$ for $s$ to be the convolution of this distribution with the MAP uncertainties assuming the parallax SNR is above a minimum SNR threshold $\varpi_{\rm SNR}^{\rm min}$ and uniform otherwise:

$$ \mathcal{L}_{s}(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\begin{cases}1&\hat{\varpi}/\sigma_{\varpi}<\varpi_{\rm SNR}^{\rm min}\\
\mathcal{N}\left[{\mu_{\varpi^{2}}},{\sigma_{\varpi^{2}}^{2}+\sigma_{s}^{2}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\right]&\hat{\varpi}/\sigma_{\varpi}\geq\varpi_{\rm SNR}^{\rm min}\end{cases} $$

We find $\varpi_{\rm SNR}^{\rm min}=4$ to be a reasonable threshold where this approximation remains valid to $\sim 10\%$ .

After applying these two terms to the photometric likelihoods computed from our earlier steps, we then select the small subset of models (often $\lesssim 1\%$ of the original grid) with expected posterior probabilities greater than $f_{\rm post}=0.005$ that of the maximum computed value. We then perform the Monte Carlo integration and resampling procedure described in §B.4 using $n_{\rm prior}=50$ samples per selected model and saving a total of $n_{\rm post}=250$ posterior samples.

#### B.6.4 Runtime

Overall, we find that for grids with $n\sim 7.5\times 10^{5}$ models, brutus is able to perform full posterior estimation in $\lesssim 5-10$ seconds when fitting $\sim 5-10$ bands of photometry with low-to-moderate SNR parallax measurements. This is comparable to the “rough” version of StarHorse described in Anders et al. [1] while giving continuous resolution in the extrinsic parameters $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ and reasonable resolution over the intrisic stellar parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ (see §IV).

Due to the adaptive thresholding, Monte Carlo (re)sampling, and use of parallax measurements, the scaling tends to be non-linear in the number of bands and the size of the grid. For smaller grids of $n\sim 4\times 10^{4}$ elements (as in §IV.2), the typical runtime is $\sim 1$ second, while for much larger grids of $n\sim 2\times 10^{6}$ elements the typical runtime can range from $\sim 20-40$ seconds. With tight parallax constraints, runtimes can be up to an order of magnitude faster (down to $\sim 0.1$ seconds).

## Appendix D Cluster Modeling

We build up the basic components of our cluster model below. In §D.1, we outline our baseline model. In §D.2, we introduce our approach for modeling unresolved (non-interacting) binaries. In §D.3, we describe our approach for dealing with cluster contamination and/or alternate stellar populations. In §D.4, we describe the additional parameters used to add empirical corrections to underlying isochrones derived from the MIST models. We finally describe additional empirical photometric corrections in §D.5.

### D.1 Baseline Model

Assuming that an open cluster can be effectively approximated by a simple stellar population (SSP), all stars in the cluster have identical initial metallicities ${\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init}$ and ages $t_{\rm age}$ but have initial masses $M_{\rm init}$ that have been independently sampled from the stellar IMF. We further assume that stars are located at approximately the same distance $d$ and are co-spatial on the sky that they are behind the same screen of dust (i.e. all have the same $A_{V}$ and $R_{V}$ ). We will collectively refer to these “cluster-level” parameters as $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ . The log-posterior over $n$ photometric sources $\{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ is then proportional to the product of the likelihoods and priors for each source plus the prior over the cluster-level parameters:

$$ \displaystyle P(\{M_{{\rm init},i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}|\{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}) \displaystyle\propto\pi(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i}(M_{{\rm init},i}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\pi(M_{{\rm init},i}) \displaystyle\equiv\pi_{\rm cluster}\times\prod_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{L}_{i}\times\pi_{i} $$

We want the likelihoods of each individual source to incorporate information from various sources when available without implicitly favoring objects with greater/fewer measurements. As a result, we consider our likelihood for each object to follow the $\chi^{2}$ -distribution, which is substantially less sensitive compared to the Normal distribution to changes in dimensionality. Our likelihood is then defined as

$$ \mathcal{L}_{i}\equiv\frac{(\chi^{2}_{i})^{k_{i}/2-1}\,e^{-\chi^{2}_{i}/2}}{2^{k_{i}/2}\,\Gamma(k_{i}/2)} $$

where $k_{i}$ is the effective number of data points ( $b_{i}$ bands of photometry plus an optional parallax measurement), $\Gamma(\cdot)$ is the Gamma function, and

$$ \chi^{2}_{i}\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{b_{i}}\frac{(\hat{F}_{i,j}-F_{i,j})^{2}}{\sigma_{F,i,j}^{2}}+\frac{(\hat{\varpi}_{i}-1/d)^{2}}{\sigma_{\varpi,i}^{2}} $$

is the “standard” $\chi^{2}$ -statistic as a function of the model photometry $\mathbf{F}_{i}$ for each object $i$ given $M_{{\rm init},i}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ .

For our baseline model, we assume that our prior is uniform within some specific range of allowed $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ and $M_{\rm init}$ values such that $\pi_{\rm cluster}$ and $\{\pi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ are constant. While this assumption is not entirely accurate (e.g., it does not apply constraints from the IMF), it drastically simplifies the problem since in practice we do not know $\{M_{{\rm init},i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ or other associated parameters for each source. While proper inference requires utilizing a full hierarchical model [112, 21, 110, e.g.,] to estimate both $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ and $\{M_{{\rm init},i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n}$ , we instead simply marginalize over the latter to get

$$ \displaystyle P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}|\{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n})\propto\prod_{i=1}^{n}\int_{M_{\rm min}}^{M_{\rm max}}\mathcal{L}_{i}(M_{\rm init}|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\,{\rm d}M_{\rm init} $$

where $M_{\rm min}=0.3\,M_{\odot}$ (the minimum mass where the MIST models are well-behaved) and $M_{\rm max}=100\,M_{\odot}$ (the standard upper limit for the IMF).

As described in Dotter [25], isochrones are more evenly sampled in EEP than in $M_{\rm init}$ . As a result, we opt to evaluate this integral using a grid in ${\rm EEP}$ . Similar to §IV.1.1, we account for the unequal spacing in $M_{\rm init}$ using second-order numerical derivatives in $\Delta M_{\rm init}/\Delta{\rm EEP}$ . By default, we use a grid of $n=2000$ evenly-spaced values between ${\rm EEP}=202$ and $808$ , which spans the beginning of the MS to the beginning of the thermally-pulsing asymptotic giant branch.

We wish to note that the approach taken here is substantially different from the analysis of binned “Hess Diagrams” commonly used in the literature [23, 24, 22, 114, 42, 40, see, e.g.,]. While the current approach requires simpler models, it has the benefit of not being sensitive to any issues related to binning over the CMD and can jointly model all observed bands rather than just 2-3 at a time. More complex star formation histories beyond SSPs can also be explored through the use of, e.g., inhomogeneous Poisson processes [67, see, e.g.,], although we defer any such improvements to future work.

This baseline model is shown in the first panel of Figure 10.

### D.2 Binaries

As clusters display prominent binary sequences, we explicitly consider the case where a given source could be an unresolved binary with a primary mass of $M_{\rm init}$ and a binary companion with secondary mass fraction $q\in[0,1]$ , where $q=0$ is equivalent to a single source and $q=1$ is an equal-mass binary. Marginalizing over both $M_{\rm init}$ and $q$ then gives

$$ \displaystyle P(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}|\{\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{i=n})\propto\prod_{i=1}^{n}\int_{M_{\rm min}}^{M_{\rm max}}\int_{0}^{1}\mathcal{L}_{i}(M_{\rm init},q|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\pi(M_{\rm init},q|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\,{\rm d}M_{\rm init}\,{\rm d}q $$

We evaluate this integral in $q$ using an adaptively-spaced grid of $n=14$ values from $q=0$ to $1$ with a resolution that ranges from $\Delta q=0.2$ near the edges to $\Delta q=0.05$ around $q=0.6$ .

Compared to §D.1, incorporating binaries involves dealing with a few additional subtleties. First, we only can model binaries down to $M_{\rm min}$ . This means that while the likelihood for $q=0$ (i.e. a single star) is defined, the likelihood from $0<q<M_{\rm min}/M_{\rm init}$ is undefined. Second, close (unresolved) binaries generally only exist when the primary (higher-mass) binary companion has not yet evolved off the MS, since this process tends to decouple the system. As a result, our likelihood as a function of $q>0$ is only defined for systems with ${\rm EEP}<480$ (i.e. before the first ascent up the giant branch). Our prior therefore becomes

$$ \displaystyle\pi \displaystyle(M_{\rm init},q|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster})\propto\begin{cases}1&\underset{{\rm Single}}{\underbrace{q=0}}\>{\rm or}\>\underset{{\rm Binary\>System}}{\underbrace{\left(\frac{M_{\rm min}}{M_{\rm init}}\leq q\leq 1\>{\rm and}\>{\rm EEP}<480\right)}}\\
0&{\rm otherwise}\end{cases} $$

where ${\rm EEP}$ again is a function of $M_{\rm init}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ .

A representation of the impact including binaries has on our cluster model is shown in the second panel of Figure 10.

### D.3 Outliers

In addition to the $\chi^{2}$ likelihood defined above, clusters are subject to additional contamination due to background/foreground field stars, which are not associated with the assumed SSP. In addition, clusters can also have populations such as blue stragglers [93] whose stellar evolution has been influenced by interactions with a companion, violating our basic SSP assumption. To account for these outliers, we modify our likelihood for each object to be a weighted mixture of two components such that

$$ \mathcal{L}_{i}(f_{\rm out}|p_{{\rm in},i})=p_{{\rm in},i}\times\mathcal{L}_{{\rm in},i}+(1-p_{{\rm in},i})\times\mathcal{L}_{{\rm out},i} $$

Here, $p_{{\rm in},i}$ is the probability that object $i$ is well-modeled by our SSP (i.e. an “inlier”) and $1-p_{\rm in}$ is the probability that it is not (i.e. an “outlier”).

The inlier probability

$$ p_{{\rm in},i}(p_{{\rm mem},i},f_{\rm out})=p_{{\rm mem},i}\times(1-f_{\rm out}) $$

is defined to be a mixture of two things. The first is the cluster membership probability $p_{{\rm mem,i}}$ for object $i$ based on possible external information such as spatial position and/or proper motion. The second is the baseline outlier fraction $f_{\rm out}$ , which governs the fraction of objects for which our outlier model $\mathcal{L}_{{\rm out},i}>\mathcal{L}_{{\rm in},i}$ serves as a better model than our inlier model (i.e. an SSP). This is a free parameter that we are interested in modeling in addition to the cluster parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ .

We take our outlier model to be an adaptive threshold such that our likelihood is constant

$$ \mathcal{L}_{{\rm out},i}(k_{i})\equiv\mathcal{L}_{{\rm in},i}(\chi^{2}_{\rm max}(k_{i}),k_{i}) $$

where the value of the likelihood is defined at the point where the cumulative probability of our $\chi^{2}$ -distribution with $k_{i}$ degrees of freedom is less than a particular threshold $p_{\rm min}$ :

$$ \int_{\chi^{2}_{\rm max}(k_{i})}^{\infty}\mathcal{L}_{{\rm in},i}(\chi^{2}_{i},k_{i})\,{\rm d}\chi^{2}_{i}=p_{\rm min} $$

This scheme is functionally equivalent to a Bayesian version of “sigma-clipping” for a given $p_{\rm min}$ with two main exceptions:

- 1. The threshold used is not a constant value but depends on the number of bands $k_{i}$ observed for each object $i$ .

- 2. An individual object’s contribution to the overall likelihood is de-emphasized rather than being completely ignored.

We set $p_{\rm min}=10^{-5}$ by default, a conservative value which corresponds to $\sim 4.5$ -sigma clipping.

A representation of the impact of outlier modeling on our cluster model is shown in the third panel of Figure 10.

### D.4 Empirical Isochrone Corrections

While the above model allows us to incorporate most of the behavior seen in open clusters (excluding the impact of rotation) such as binarity (§D.2) and outliers (§D.3), it does not account for systematic modeling issues in the SSP itself as derived from theoretical isochrones such as MIST and the use of synthetic spectra such as those derived from the C3K models. We use a series of empirically-motivated corrections (see §V.1) to the underlying isochrones in order to address some of these issues. Note that these are common across all theoretical isochrones, not just MIST, with the exception of specialized grids designed to specifically tackle particular problems.

Our corrections work by adding an additional set of “corrected” surface-level parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\star}^{\prime}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\star},\boldsymbol{\theta})$ that are a function of the original predicted surface-level parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\star}$ as well as the underlying stellar evolution parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ from the MIST isochrones. In particular, we opt to modify the stellar radius $\log R_{\star}$ and the effective temperature $\log T_{\rm eff}$ (and by proxy the surface gravity $\log g$ and bolometric luminosity $\log L_{\rm bol}$ ) such that

$$ \begin{bmatrix}M_{\rm init}\\
{\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init}\\
t_{\rm age}\end{bmatrix}\xrightarrow{}\begin{bmatrix}\log g\\
\log T_{\rm eff}\\
\log L_{\rm bol}\\
\log R_{\star}\\
{\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm surf}\end{bmatrix}\xrightarrow{}\begin{bmatrix}\log g^{\prime}\\
\log T_{\rm eff}^{\prime}\\
\log L_{\rm bol}^{\prime}\\
\log R_{\star}^{\prime}\\
{\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm surf}\end{bmatrix}\xrightarrow{}\begin{bmatrix}M_{1}\\
\vdots\\
M_{b}\end{bmatrix} $$

We choose to apply empirical corrections to $\log R_{\star}$ and $\log T_{\rm eff}$ for two reasons. The first is that we expect both to be strongly affected by magnetic fields, which appear to “puff up” stars, making them larger, and contribute to sunspot activity, making them cooler overall [8, 105, 104]. Magnetic activity tends to increase at lower masses, leading to substantial deviations in the observed properties of stars compared to predictions from models such as MIST which does not take these effects into account. The second reason we choose to apply corrections in this domain is that detailed modeling of binaries already suggests that the MIST models deviate slightly from the observations in these two domains [18].

To keep our empirical corrections as simple as possible, we only introduce corrections for masses below $M_{\rm init}=1\,M_{\odot}$ and “suppress” the effects of our derived corrections after stars evolve off the MS (i.e. after stars have ${\rm EEP}>454$ ) and for sub-solar metallicities (where the fits are relatively unconstrained; see §V.2). We further assume that our corrections only involve a single parameter, $M_{\rm init}$ , and that they are fully linear. While we experimented with more complex functional forms, we found that there was not enough data to warrant using them. Note that these corrections do not deal in any way with evolved stars, such as the red clump and horizontal giant branch. While there are known disagreements between the MIST models and observations at those particular stellar evolutionary phases [18], investigating them is beyond the scope of this work.

Altogether, we end up modeling variations in $\Delta\log T_{\rm eff}\equiv\log T_{\rm eff}^{\prime}-\log T_{\rm eff}$ and $\Delta\log R_{\star}\equiv\log R_{\star}^{\prime}-\log R_{\star}$ using

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\log T_{\rm eff}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \displaystyle=f_{T}(M_{\rm init})\times g({\rm EEP})\times h({\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init}) \displaystyle\Delta\log R_{\star}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \displaystyle=f_{R}(M_{\rm init})\times g({\rm EEP})\times h({\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init}) $$

We then propagate these modifications to derive relative corrections $\Delta\log g\equiv\log g^{\prime}-\log g$ and $\Delta\log L_{\rm bol}(T_{\rm eff}^{\prime})\equiv\log L_{\rm bol}^{\prime}(T_{\rm eff}^{\prime})-\log L_{\rm bol}(T_{\rm eff}^{\prime})$ via

$$ \displaystyle\Delta\log g \displaystyle=-2\times\Delta\log R_{\star} \displaystyle\Delta\log L_{\rm bol}(T_{\rm eff}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=2\times\Delta\log R_{\star} $$

Our corrections in $\Delta\log T_{\rm eff}$ and $\Delta\log R_{\star}$ have three components. The first, $f_{T}(M_{\rm init})$ and $f_{R}(M_{\rm init})$ , represent the “baseline” shifts in effective temperature and radius, respectively, and are defined to be piece-wise linear functions of $M_{\rm init}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle f_{T}(M_{\rm init}) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\log\left[1+c_{T}\times(M_{\rm init}-1)\right]&M_{\rm init}<1\,M_{\odot}\\
0&M_{\rm init}\geq 1\,M_{\odot}\end{cases} \displaystyle f_{R}(M_{\rm init}) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}\log\left[1+c_{R}\times(M_{\rm init}-1)\right]&M_{\rm init}<1\,M_{\odot}\\
0&M_{\rm init}\geq 1\,M_{\odot}\end{cases} $$

where $c_{T}$ and $c_{R}$ can be seen as characterizing the (fractional) offset in $T_{\rm eff}$ and $R_{\star}$ , respectively, as a function of $M_{\rm init}$ . The second, $g({\rm EEP}$ , represents a “suppression” term that reduces the offsets as stars evolve off the MS. We take this to be a modified logistic function

$$ g({\rm EEP})=1-\frac{1}{1+\exp\left[-({\rm EEP}-454)/\Delta_{\rm EEP}\right]} $$

where $\Delta_{\rm EEP}$ sets the EEP scale over which this suppression takes place. This function strictly decreases from $1\rightarrow 0$ as a star evolves off the MS. Finally, $h({\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init})$ represents an additional “suppression” term that reduces the offsets at sub-solar metallicities. We take this to be a simple exponential

$$ h({\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init})=\exp\left(A_{\rm{\rm[Fe/H]}}\times{\rm[Fe/H]}_{\rm init}\right) $$

where $A_{{\rm[Fe/H]}}$ sets the amplitude of the suppression ( $1/A_{{\rm[Fe/H]}}$ can also be thought of as a scale). We note that while this function does suppress contributions at sub-solar metallicities, it actually give a slight enhancement for super-solar metallicites. The tests performed in §V.2 and §V.3 did not provide enough evidence to support/refute this effect, and so we opted to leave it in for simplicity.

While we consider $c_{T}$ and $c_{R}$ as free parameters we are interested in modeling in addition to the cluster parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ , we find we do not have enough data to model $\Delta_{\rm EEP}$ and $A_{{\rm[Fe/H]}}$ reliably. After experimenting with a variety of values using the data described in §V.2 as well as observations of Ruprecht 106 taken from Dotter et al. [27], we ultimately set $\Delta_{\rm EEP}=30$ and $A_{{\rm[Fe/H]}}=0.5$ . See Table 4 for a summary of the parameters used to model empirical corrections used in this work and their final set of values.

A representation of the impact these empirical corrections have on our cluster model is shown in the fourth panel of Figure 10. An illustration of the functional forms used for the corrections themselves is shown in Figure 9. We find that the overall empirical corrections substantially improve behavior down to $M_{\rm init}\sim 0.5\,M_{\odot}$ , which can be seen more clearly in Figure 11 and §E.

### D.5 Empirical Photometric Corrections

Although we find the set of empirical corrections outlined in §D.4 substantially improve the overall shape and overall offset of the MIST isochrones relative to data from nearby open clusters, they are unable to address overall offsets in photometry that might come from, e.g., slightly different photometric calibrations between the synthetic photometry computed from models versus the real photometry from surveys (such as in the Vega system) or issues with the C3K stellar atmosphere models. Both of these manifest themselves, to first order, as photometric offsets between the model predictions and the observed data.

We model these offsets explicitly by introducing a set of scale-factors $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}=\{s_{{\rm em},i}\}_{i=1}^{i=b}$ that simply rescale the data such that the new flux density $\hat{F}_{i,j}^{\prime}$ for a given star $i$ in band $j$ is

$$ \hat{F}_{i,j}^{\prime}=s_{{\rm em},j}\times\hat{F}_{i,j} $$

We treat $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}$ as $b$ free parameters that we are interested in modeling in addition to the cluster parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\rm cluster}$ . We are able to do so thanks to the large number of available parallax measurements from Gaia DR2 that give independent constraints on the distance, thereby fixing not just offsets in color but offsets in absolute magnitude.

Our final cluster model after including these additional empirical corrections is shown in the fifth panel of Figure 10.

## Appendix F Estimating Photometric Offsets from Field Stars

We aim to estimate $s_{{\rm em},j}$ in each band $j$ by computing the ratio of the observed flux $\hat{F}_{i,j}$ for star $i$ to the predicted flux $F_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ . This will be averaged over the posterior $P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i,\setminus j},\hat{\varpi}_{i})$ , estimated from the measured flux densities excluding band $j$ $\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i,\setminus j}$ for each individual source. Averaging across all $n$ sources then gives:

$$ s_{{\rm em},j}\approx\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int\frac{F_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})}{\hat{F}_{i,j}}P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i,\setminus j},\hat{\varpi}_{i}){\rm d}\boldsymbol{\theta}{\rm d}\boldsymbol{\phi} $$

*Figure 25: Residual magnitude offsets within the Bayestar models in the Pan-STARRS (top) and 2MASS (bottom) data over the “benchmark” field star sample (Figure 12) after correcting for mean photometric offsets using the procedure described in §V.3. The top row of each set of figures shows the normalized density of stars as a function of $\Delta{\rm mag}$ versus observed magnitude in each band, while the bottom row shows the corresponding offset as a function of position on the Gaia $G$ versus $BP-RP$ CMD from Figure 12. Since the empirical Bayestar models were originally constructed using both Pan-STARRS and 2MASS photometry, as expected the overall offsets are small ( $\lesssim 1\%$ ) and only display weak trends as a function of magnitude and position of the CMD.*

Naively, computing this would require generating $b$ sets of $n$ posteriors (excluding each band in turn). Instead, we opt to simply reweight the samples from the single set of $n$ posteriors $P(F_{i,j}|\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i},\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ computed using all the bands. Assuming that each source $i$ has a set of $m$ samples $\{(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,1},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,1}),\dots,(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,m},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,m})\}\sim P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i},\hat{\varpi}_{i})$ from the underlying posterior, our estimate then becomes

$$ s_{{\rm em},j}\approx\frac{1}{nm}\frac{1}{\hat{F}_{i,j}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{m}w_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})\,F_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})}{\sum_{k=1}^{m}w_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})} $$

where the importance weights $w_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})$ are defined as

$$ w_{i,j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})=\frac{P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}}_{i,\setminus j},\hat{\varpi}_{i})}{P(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi}|\hat{\mathbf{F}_{i}},\hat{\varpi}_{i})}=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{{\rm phot},\setminus j}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})}{\mathcal{L}_{\rm phot}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{i,k},\boldsymbol{\phi}_{i,k})} $$

where $\mathcal{L}_{{\rm phot},\setminus j}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\boldsymbol{\phi})$ is the photometric likelihood excluding band $j$ . Since computing the photometric likelihoods with and without band $j$ is trivial, this procedure offers a much more computationally efficient way to estimate photometric offsets.

*Figure 26: As Figure 25, but now showing the residual magnitude offsets within the MIST models in the Gaia DR2 (top), Pan-STARRS, and 2MASS+AllWISE (bottom) data. Compared to the Bayestar models (Figure 25), the offsets here are substantially larger ( $\sim 3\%$ ) and display strong trends as a function of magnitude and position of the CMD, especially in the bluest and reddest bands.*

We make three small changes when applying the above strategy in practice:

- 1. Rather than strictly using the weighted mean of the entire sample, we compute the median of weighted mean estimates from jackknife realizations ( $n=1000$ ) in order to be less sensitive to possible outliers.

- 2. We apply a Gaussian prior over $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}$ with a mean of $1$ and standard deviation of $0.01$ in each band to avoid behavior where a combination of (large) offsets can become degenerate with adjusting entire intrinsic stellar types. We incorporate this into the initial estimate of $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}$ computed above by using bootstrapping to estimate errors in our initial estimate and assuming the PDF is Gaussian.

- 3. We repeat the process iteratively by applying the $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}$ estimated from the previous stage before computing new estimates of the posteriors. We consider our results converged when each element of $\mathbf{s}_{\rm em}$ changes by less than $\sim 0.01$ .

We investigate the impact various assumptions can have on recovery of extrinsic parameters $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ , in particular distance $d$ and extinction $A_{V}$ . To do this, we decide to model a subsample of stars in sightlines towards the Orion star forming complex taken from Zucker & Speagle et al. [120]. For each star, we model the 8-band SED (Pan-STARRS and 2MASS) along with the measured parallax from Gaia DR2 under four different assumptions:

- • Case 1: We emulate the setup used in Green et al. [44] when deriving the 3-D Bayestar19 dust map, where the underlying stellar models are the Bayestar models the $R_{V}$ is fixed to a value of $3.3$ , and there is no 3-D dust prior applied.

- • Case 2: As above, but now allowing $R_{V}$ to vary subject to the prior described in §A.6. This emulates the setup from Zucker & Speagle et al. [120] and Zucker et al. [119].

- • Case 3: As above, but now using the MIST models instead of the Bayestar models. This approximates the setup in Cargile et al. [15], where the 3-D dust extinction prior is extremely weak.

- • Case 4: As above, but now with the full 3-D Bayestar19 dust map prior applied. This is the default setup in brutus.

The results of each of these tests for a representative subsample of stars that were well-fit in all four cases is shown in Figure 27. While we find some stars do not exhibit many changes in their inferred distance modulus $\mu$ or extinction $A_{V}$ , we do find large variations for many sources. Some of these can be attributed to $R_{V}$ variation, such as with source 3, which shows a substantial change in $A_{V}$ linked to shifts in $R_{V}$ and changes in the inferred intrinsic parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as a result. We also see substantial changes for a number of sources when moving from the Bayestar to the MIST models, many of which are either caused by changes in stellar type or by additional solutions now made available due to the increased diversity of allowed stellar models (see Figure 8). Finally, we see that the 3-D dust extinction prior serves as a strong constraint in many cases, with the inferred $\mu$ and $A_{V}$ constraints both shifting around and tightening considerably. These results, along with the degeneracies discussed in §VI.1, highlight the importance of obtaining strong constraints on the dust extinction towards various sources in order to be confident that the inferred $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ for various stars are both well-constrained and accurate.

We also perform an additional test with an alternate codebase designed to more closely emulate the setup (modeling, priors, etc.) used in Schlafly et al. [97] and Green et al. [44]. The differences between the two approaches were minimal and could primarily be traced back to differences in the Galactic prior.
